title: Composting: Turning Waste into Soil
summary: How tiny decomposers, worms, air, and water turn food scraps and dry leaves into rich compost that feeds plants and keeps food out of landfills.
poll: Every home should compost its food scraps.

versions.title: Turning Scraps into Soil
versions.text:
Do not throw out your food scraps! You can turn them into rich, dark soil. This soil is called compost.

Put scraps in a heap or a bin. Use fruit and plant peels. Add dry leaves. Add bits of old paper, too. Do not add meat or milk. They smell bad. They bring pests.

Tiny live things make the heap rot. Most are too small to see. Worms help, too. They eat the scraps. The scraps break down.

A heap needs air. It needs a bit of water, too. Mix it now and then. That lets air in. The heap gets warm in the middle!

In a few months, the heap looks like soil. It smells like a wet field. Mix it into the ground. Plants grow well in it. It helps dry, sandy land hold water. That is good in hot lands like Saudi Arabia.

When food goes to the dump, it is just waste. Compost helps the land. It is a smart way to use what we do not eat.

When food goes to the dump, it is just waste. When we make compost, we give it back to the land.

versions.title: Composting: Turning Waste into Soil
versions.text:
What happens to the peels after you eat a banana or an orange? In many homes, they go straight into the trash. But food scraps do not have to be waste. They can become compost, a rich, dark material that gardeners love.

To make compost, people collect scraps in a pile or a special bin. Gardeners often talk about two kinds of ingredients. "Greens" are wet, fresh things such as fruit and vegetable peels, coffee grounds, and grass. "Browns" are dry things such as dead leaves, straw, and pieces of cardboard. A good pile has a mix of both. Meat, milk, and oily food should stay out, because they smell bad and attract pests.

The real work is done by decomposers. These are living things that break down dead plants and animals. Most are bacteria and fungi, which are too small to see. Worms and insects help by chewing the scraps into smaller pieces.

Decomposers need air and water. The pile should be moist, like a sponge that has been squeezed out. Turning it every week or two adds fresh air. As the bacteria work, they give off heat, and the center of a large pile can become hot.

After a few months, the pile turns into dark, crumbly compost that smells like a forest floor. It is full of nutrients, the substances plants need to grow. Compost also helps sandy soil hold water, which is valuable in dry places like Saudi Arabia.

Composting helps in another way, too. When food is buried in a landfill, it rots without air and releases a gas called methane, which helps trap heat around the Earth. Composting keeps food out of landfills and turns it into something useful.

versions.title: Composting: Turning Waste into Soil
versions.text:
What happens to the peels after you finish a banana or an orange? In many households, they travel directly into the garbage; however, food scraps need not become waste. Instead, they can be transformed into compost, a rich, dark material that gardeners and farmers value tremendously.

To produce compost, people collect scraps in a pile or a specially designed container. Gardeners typically describe two categories of ingredients. "Greens" are moist, fresh materials such as fruit and vegetable peels, coffee grounds, and grass clippings, and they are rich in nitrogen. "Browns" are dry materials such as fallen leaves, straw, and shredded cardboard, which are rich in carbon. A productive pile contains a careful balance of both. Meat, dairy products, and oily food should be excluded, because they generate unpleasant odors and attract unwanted pests.

The essential work is performed by decomposers, organisms that break down dead plants and animals, and most are microorganisms, such as bacteria and fungi, which are invisible without a microscope. Worms and insects contribute by chewing the scraps into smaller fragments, which gives the microorganisms more surface to consume.

Decomposers require both oxygen and moisture. The pile should remain damp, similar to a sponge that has been squeezed out, and turning it every week or two supplies additional oxygen. As the bacteria digest the material, they release energy as heat, and the center of a large pile can exceed sixty degrees Celsius, which destroys many weed seeds and harmful germs.

After several months, the pile becomes dark, crumbly compost that smells like a forest floor. It is full of nutrients, the substances that plants require for healthy growth. Compost also improves the ability of sandy soil to retain water, which is especially valuable in dry regions such as Saudi Arabia.

Composting benefits the environment in another significant way. When food is buried in a landfill, it decays without oxygen and releases methane, a greenhouse gas that traps heat in the atmosphere. Composting diverts food from landfills and converts it into a valuable resource.

versions.title: Composting: Turning Waste into Soil
versions.text:
What happens to the peels after you finish a banana or an orange? In many households, they travel directly into the garbage; however, food scraps need not become waste; instead, they can be transformed into compost, a rich, dark material that gardeners and farmers value tremendously.

To produce compost, people accumulate scraps in a pile or a specially designed container. Gardeners typically describe two categories of ingredients. "Greens" are moist, fresh materials such as fruit and vegetable peels, coffee grounds, and grass clippings, and they are rich in nitrogen. "Browns" are dry materials such as fallen leaves, straw, and shredded cardboard, which are rich in carbon. A productive pile contains a deliberate balance of both. Meat, dairy products, and oily food should be excluded, because they generate unpleasant odors and attract unwanted pests.

The essential work is performed by decomposers, organisms that break down dead plants and animals, and most are microorganisms, such as bacteria and fungi, which are invisible without a microscope. Worms and insects contribute by chewing the scraps into smaller fragments, which provides the microorganisms with additional surface area to consume.

Decomposers require both oxygen and moisture, so the pile should remain damp, similar to a sponge that has been squeezed out, and turning it periodically supplies additional oxygen. As the bacteria digest the material, they release energy as heat, and the interior of a large pile can exceed sixty degrees Celsius, temperatures that destroy many weed seeds and harmful germs.

After several months, the pile becomes dark, crumbly compost that smells like a forest floor. Scientists describe the stable, dark substance in finished compost as humus, which binds soil particles together and gradually releases nutrients over many seasons. It is full of nutrients, the substances that plants require for vigorous growth. Compost also improves the capacity of sandy soil to retain water, an especially valuable quality in arid regions such as Saudi Arabia.

Composting benefits the environment in another significant way, because when food is buried in a landfill, it decomposes without oxygen and releases methane, a powerful greenhouse gas that traps heat in the atmosphere. Composting therefore diverts food from landfills and converts it into a valuable agricultural resource.

keyWords.definition: the top layer of the ground where plants grow

keyWords.definition: things that are thrown away because people do not want them
keyWords.example: Our class tries to make less waste at lunch.

keyWords.definition: a small, long animal with a soft body and no legs that lives in the ground

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to cook tasty meals with fruit peels
How food scraps can be turned into soil
Why so many worms live in the desert
How to build a trash dump
questions.why: The article explains how scraps, worms, air, and water make compost, a rich soil that helps plants.

wrong.A: The article does not talk about cooking.
wrong.C: Worms help make compost, but the article is not about where worms live.
wrong.D: The dump is mentioned, but the article does not explain how to build one.

wrong.A: Fruit peels are good to add.
wrong.B: Dry leaves are good to add.
wrong.C: Bits of paper are good to add.

questions.stem: What helps the food scraps break down?
options: Worms and tiny living things

wrong.C: Ice and snow are not part of compost.

questions.stem: The article says tiny living things make the scraps rot. What does rot mean?
options: Freeze solid
Grow taller
Slowly break down
Turn bright blue

questions.stem: Why should you mix or turn a compost heap now and then?
options: To make it smell bad
To keep the worms out
To let air in
To make it cold

wrong.A: Turning the heap is not meant to make it smell bad.
wrong.B: Worms help the heap, so we do not want them out.
wrong.D: The middle of the heap gets warm, and turning is for air.

questions.stem: Why would a gardener in a hot, dry place want compost?
options: It helps soil hold water for plants.
It keeps the hot sun away from the land.
It makes rain fall.
It turns sand into rock.
questions.why: The article says compost helps dry, sandy land hold water, which plants need in hot places.

wrong.D: Compost does not turn sand into rock.

questions.stem: The middle of a compost heap feels warm. What does this most likely show?
options: Someone lit a fire in it.
The sun is shining inside it.
Rats are sleeping deep inside it.
The tiny living things are at work.

wrong.A: No one lights a fire in a compost heap.
wrong.B: The sun cannot shine inside the middle of a heap.
wrong.C: Rats are pests that people try to keep away.
